This essay asks whose interests count when a river's water is allocated. The case is the Okavango Delta. No mark scheme is attached. The answer uses only interests that the opened sources give as reasons, and an interest they do not discuss stays outside it. Several sources could be kept only as abstracts, because the official address did not return a real PDF. One book chapter was opened in full. A claim that rests on an abstract does not go past that abstract, and a figure the chapter only cites from another work is not treated as a measurement this essay made.

An interest, here, is a reason a gathered source gives for caring how the river's water is shared. The sources do not share one definition and they do not rank the reasons. Bauer‐Gottwein, Gumbricht and Kinzelbach (2006) frame a balance between human and environmental water demands. King, Beuster, Brown and Joubert (2014) describe costs and benefits for the river ecosystem, social structures, and local and national economies. compares climate pressure with a local development scenario. Phonchi-Tshekiso, Sitas and Selomane (2024),, and Gondo, Kolawole, Mbaiwa and Motsholapheko (2020) write from villages and livelihoods. argue that conflicts of interest across scales are part of environmental injustice. Counting an interest means one of these texts gives it as a reason. It does not mean a fair share or a winner has been found.

The river itself is the first reason the modelling abstracts give. Bauer‐Gottwein, Gumbricht and Kinzelbach (2006) describe an endorheic system. Runoff generated in the humid tropical highlands of Angola flows through arid Namibia and Botswana, forms a large inland delta, and is eventually consumed by evapotranspiration. They give the delta an approximate size of about 30,000 square kilometres and call it the world's largest site protected under the 1971 Ramsar convention on wetlands. They say the extended wetlands sustain a rich ecology, spectacular wildlife, and a first-class tourism infrastructure, and that those wetlands depend on highly seasonal runoff in the Okavango River together with variable local climate. Annual fluctuations in inflow become vast areas of seasonally inundated floodplain. On that description, the delta is not a store of spare water. It is the place where the river's water is used up by the wetland. An allocation upstream is therefore already an allocation of the flood that the delta would otherwise receive.

The same abstract says that water abstraction and reservoir building in the upstream countries are expected to reduce or redistribute the flows available to the delta. To study upstream and local interventions, the authors built a coupled surface-water and groundwater model on a one-square-kilometre grid. Floodplain data are sparse, so the model was compared with satellite flooding patterns rather than with point hydrographs. The abstract says the scenario results can help decision makers balance environmental and human water demands. The scenario magnitudes are not in the abstract, so they are not used. What the abstract does establish is a pair of interests: environmental demand, seen as flood extent, and human demand, including upstream abstraction and reservoirs. Both are reasons a decision has to weigh. Neither is given a number here.

King, Beuster, Brown and Joubert (2014) place that weighing across borders. Their abstract says the river flows through Angola, Namibia, and Botswana, is in near-natural condition, and supports iconic wetlands and wildlife, while the basin's people are poor and development is inevitable. The member states completed a transboundary diagnostic analysis in 2010, funded by the three governments and the Global Environment Facility. A central feature was a basin-wide environmental flow assessment using DRIFT, Downstream Response to Imposed Flow Transformation. The abstract says the scenarios of increasing water-resource use spelled out costs and benefits for the river ecosystem, for associated social structures, and for local and national economies, and that those results helped create a strategic action programme the states were beginning to act on. Only the abstract was opened, so the findings are not reported here as figures. The interests the assessment was built to count are still clear: the river ecosystem, the social structures tied to it, and economies at local and national scale. Upstream development is called inevitable. It is not treated as the only interest. The hope that the river could illustrate the three pillars of sustainable development is a stated aim, not a result this essay can check.

 adds climate as a separate pressure. The thesis abstract models hydrology and vegetation for 2050–2080 and 2070–2100 under the IPCC A2 scenario and five climate models, and it compares those runs with a local development scenario. Past runoff, rainfall, and potential evapotranspiration were modified and passed through a hydrological model. The simulations predict drying, with deeper groundwater and less frequent inundation. Climate change is expected to matter more, in these runs, than regional development. Deforestation along the river is said to increase inflow and so to mitigate the local climate effect. Vegetation types had distinct preferred groundwater depths, wetter types are expected to lose area, and biodiversity is expected to decline because many wet types are not widely spread. A closing acknowledgement thanks a supervisor. It is not a finding and it does not add an author. For the question of whose interests count, the abstract treats inundation and groundwater as conditions that can be lost, and it warns that a local development plan is not the only change the delta faces. It does not give any user a present-day share of the river.

The village studies name local interests, and they are not one interest repeated. Phonchi-Tshekiso, Sitas and Selomane (2024) interviewed 116 people in Etsha 6, Khwai, and Tubu about land and water acquisitions. The abstract says that reporting only agricultural deals underplays tourism and conservation. The main drivers were tourism and subsistence agriculture. In Tubu, farmland in flood recessions was borrowed between locals, a practice the authors call land borrowing. Concessions, borrowings, and rentals were the types people perceived, with both positive and negative effects. Cultural grouping shaped people's connection with riparian waters and how land was exchanged. Disparities in benefits, the abstract says, work against equitable distribution. Only the abstract was opened. It shows that tourism operators, subsistence farmers, and people who borrow flood-recession land are already interests in how delta land and water are taken up. It does not say which group should receive a stated volume.

 reports on Seronga, at the northern edge of the delta. Agricultural production and livestock keeping remain the main subsistence for most people, while tourism and market links create a need for cash income. The abstract draws on the Future Okavango socio-economic baseline survey and says the strategies in Seronga are highly diversified, with risk tied to reliance on natural resources. Other studies named as background were not opened and are not sources here. The abstract supports a household interest in farming, livestock, and cash, in a place exposed because it depends on the delta. It does not say how much water Seronga uses, or who should give way if the river is allocated elsewhere.

Gondo, Kolawole, Mbaiwa and Motsholapheko (2020) come closer to water as a governed good inside villages. Their abstract analyses demographic and socio-economic factors in the dissonance between customary and statutory institutions, drawing on institutional bricolage and mass-elite theory. They selected Shakawe, Tubu, and Shorobe, interviewed 455 household heads, and spoke with nine key informants. The results reported in the abstract are specific. There was a gender imbalance in water collection. Consumption was relatively higher in small households than in large ones. There was no evidence that age affected consumption. Affordability, distance to sources, and the intended use of water were factors of access. Income was a key determinant of the amount of water consumed. The abstract concludes that an integrated water-governance model is needed, one that would enhance the demand and consumption of water in local communities. This essay reports that conclusion as the authors' closing claim, not as a finding that consumption ought to rise. The results that can be used are the inequalities: who collects water, how income and distance shape access, and the gap between customary and statutory rules. Those are interests that count when the river's water is allocated, because an allocation that stops at the basin border still lands in households where access is already uneven. The abstract does not give a basin share for Shakawe, Tubu, or Shorobe.

The one full text is a theological chapter, not a second model., in a volume edited by Chirongoma and Kiilu and issued by African Sun Media, argue for an environmental Christology with the delta as the case. The chapter says that treating the Earth's resources as infinite is a message coming from global, national, district, and local scales, and that the agendas at those scales have led to conflicts of interest which contribute to environmental injustice. The delta is described as giving life to wildlife and to human communities, and dry seasons are described as times when water is scarce, animals crowd what remains, and elephants break into riparian homes. The arriving flood, from the Angolan plateau, is water people meet in order to drink, wash, and renew ordinary life. The conclusion asks that the delta not be treated only as a resource for human consumption.

That argument counts non-human life, and the identity of river people, as interests. A footnote says the Hamkushu are known as river people because their way of life has revolved around the delta for centuries. The chapter names threats it attributes to human use: fertiliser runoff, poaching, climate change, and tourism. It cites for a drying prediction, which matches the thesis abstract and adds no new measurement. Tourist counts, poaching rates, and stream-flow percentages in the chapter belong to works this essay did not open, so they are not adopted as findings. What is used is the chapter's own contrast: tourism is described as income, jobs, and investment, and also as roads, disturbance, litter, and sewage in the water. The chapter is an argument, not a calibrated allocation. Its force is that a human use, at any of the four scales it names, is not the only interest that counts.

Read together, the opened texts support a bounded answer. An interest counts when one of these sources treats it as a reason for how the river's water is shared. The environmental interest counts because the 2006 modelling abstract defines the decision as a balance with environmental demand, because King, Beuster, Brown and Joubert (2014) built scenarios around the river ecosystem, and because ties vegetation to inundation and groundwater. Upstream and national development count because that modelling abstract expects abstraction and reservoirs to change the inflow, and because the flow abstract sets development beside local and national economies. Livelihoods count because Phonchi-Tshekiso, Sitas and Selomane (2024) find tourism and subsistence farming driving acquisitions, with uneven benefits, and because finds farming and livestock still carrying Seronga while cash needs grow. Households count because Gondo, Kolawole, Mbaiwa and Motsholapheko (2020) show collection, income, distance, and affordability already structuring access. Non-human life and river communities count because treat a purely human claim on an infinite supply as an injustice.

What does not follow is a winner. No opened source states a rule that would let one interest cancel the others. The modelling and flow papers, read only as abstracts, do not yield scenario tables. The village abstracts do not yield a volume or a legal entitlement. The chapter does not measure a release. Drying in may outweigh regional development in those runs, but the abstract does not say local users therefore lose their claim. Uneven benefits in Phonchi-Tshekiso, Sitas and Selomane (2024) show that naming an interest is not the same as sharing the benefit. Gender and income in Gondo, Kolawole, Mbaiwa and Motsholapheko (2020) show that an interest can count at basin scale and still fail inside the household. These interests count. The opened evidence does not authorise one ranked allocation, and the gap is not filled by a share or a finding the sources do not give.
